answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: c. 544 – c. 496 BC · Chinese general & military strategist (traditional dates)
answer.sourceLine: The teaching is genuinely Sun Tzu’s, from The Art of War, Chapter III (“Attack by Stratagem”), where Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation reads “supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.” The familiar one-liner is a faithful modern paraphrase that fuses that idea with the phrase “subdue the enemy without fighting” — it is not a verbatim line from any standard edition.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: trad. attrib. Sun Tzu, c. 5th century BC

source.excerpt: Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.
trail: Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation renders the passage as “supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting” — see Ch. III, Attack by Stratagem ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the companion line “To subdue the enemy without fighting is the acme of skill” as a genuine quote from the same chapter.
The exact popular wording circulates on Goodreads ↗ as “The supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting,” credited to The Art of War — a paraphrase, not a verbatim translation.
Modern scholarship (Wikipedia ↗) dates the text to the Warring States period and doubts “Sun Tzu” was a single historical figure.
source.cutTag: ↑ Giles’s actual 1910 wording — the popular one-liner paraphrases it
source.excerptNote: Later translations render a companion line in the same chapter as “To subdue the enemy without fighting is the acme of skill,” per Wikiquote ↗ — that phrasing supplies the ‘subdue’ verb the popular version uses.

author.name: Sun Tzu
author.heading: About Sun Tzu
author.metaLine: c. 544 – c. 496 BC · Chinese general & strategist
author.bio: Sun Tzu (Sun Wu) is the general and strategist traditionally credited as author of The Art of War, the foundational Chinese treatise on strategy. The Han historian Sima Qian placed his life around 544–496 BC, but modern scholars doubt he was a single historical figure and date the surviving text to the Warring States period — likely at least a century after his supposed lifetime. His central claim, that the highest skill is to win before battle is joined, has shaped military, political and business thinking for two millennia.

items.scope: Circulated as a verbatim translation from
items.why: No standard English edition reads this way. Giles’s 1910 text has “supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting” (Ch. III ↗); the popular line borrows ‘supreme’ from that and ‘subdue the enemy without fighting’ from a separate, later-rendered line.
Modern scholarship dates the text to the Warring States period and questions whether “Sun Tzu” was one real person, per Wikipedia ↗ — so “Sun Tzu wrote” is a convention as much as a fact.

misattribution.truthLine: The substance is real Sun Tzu — The Art of War, Chapter III — but the exact sentence is a modern paraphrase, not a line from Giles or any standard edition, as a look at the actual translation ↗ shows.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Chapter III of The Art of War is where Sun Tzu argues that the highest generalship wins before swords are drawn — by wrecking the enemy’s plans and splitting his alliances rather than smashing his armies. Taking the enemy’s state “whole and intact,” he writes, beats shattering it.

That idea — victory without battle — became the most quoted thing in the whole book, carried far beyond warfare into business, sports, negotiation and diplomacy, usually in the smoothed-out form you see here.
detailsBody: Translators have long wrestled with the original. As The Strategy Bridge ↗ notes, the Chinese 不戰 (“not battle”) may point to avoiding pitched, formally arrayed battle rather than avoiding all fighting — a nuance the tidy English one-liner tends to erase.
